Scale and detail

When using formulas or structures, check accuracy. A misplaced chemical bond or incomplete equation is especially obvious to the audience most likely to receive the gift.

Work in stitch dimensions rather than pixels alone. The same artwork may work at 120 stitches wide and lose its identity completely when reduced to 45. Color and style

Complex molecules may need simplification, but essential connectivity should remain. Do not remove atoms or bonds simply because it looks cleaner when that changes the meaning.

Limit colors deliberately. Every extra shade should add volume, separation or identity; if it appears in only a few stitches without changing the image, it may add work rather than quality. Composition and personalization

A laboratory theme does not require white and blue. Neon, retro or monochrome palettes can make the subject more decorative without losing recognition.

Think about the final use as well: gift, framed art, mini, collection or personalization. Composition should respond to the object the customer wants to finish, not only to an attractive source image. Rights and accuracy where relevant

Avoid copying university, laboratory or company logos. Science offers enough generic iconography to create original designs that are commercially safer.

When logos, photographs, artwork or third-party data are involved, use your own, licensed or clearly reusable sources. Designing original work from the beginning avoids problems and builds a stronger identity. Turning it into an original collection

We can build collections by discipline — chemistry, biology, astronomy and mathematics — while sharing one graphic language. That lets each category serve clear intent without repeating the same flask.

Our PDFs should present measurements, colors and detail level honestly.
